title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in SF: Scalable Route Search ⚡
description: Bidirectional Dijkstra runs two shortest-path searches at once—one forward from the start and one backward from the destination—until the frontiers meet. Watch how this cuts explored nodes dramatically on a dense city graph, mirroring how modern route planners scale.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale — Inside high-scale navigation engines: Bidirectional Dijkstra visualised ⚡

Two-ended search, one goal. Instead of expanding outward from only the start, we launch Dijkstra from both ends and stop early when the forward + backward best paths can’t be improved. This reduces the “visited” set on dense grids and makes the shortest path feel fast even at scale.

What to look for in the animation:
• Two frontiers expanding in opposite directions
• A meeting point where paths connect
• Fewer explored nodes vs single-source Dijkstra

Takeaway: Bidirectional search is a practical speed-up when edge weights are non-negative—especially for route planning at scale.

Debate question: Should route-planner engineers always default to bidirectional search, or are there cases where the overhead/complexity doesn’t pay off?
